newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch bank ABN profits up, but outlook cloudy.
newsitem.headline: Dutch bank ABN profits up, but outlook cloudy.

text.p: Soaring securities markets helped Dutch banking giant ABN AMRO NV, the largest foreign bank operating in the United States, unveil a 26 percent increase in 1996 net profit Thursday, but it gave mixed signals about its prospects for 1997.
Net profit rose to 3.30 billion guilders ($1.7 billion) from 2.62 billion ($1.3 billion) in 1995.
"1996 was an excellent year for the bank. All businesses contributed to the strong result," ABN AMRO said.

ABN also said it planned to list its shares in American Depositary Receipts on the New York Stock Exchange, improving its ability to raise capital from U.S. investors. It also said it planned a four-for-one stock split and a buy-back of 1 percent of its shares as part of the stock listing.
Profits were in line with analysts' forecasts but the shares weakened after the bank declined to make a forecast for the current year due to uncertainty about financial markets.
The annual results included the first disclosure of the bank's hidden reserves, which totalled 4.02 billion guilders ($2.07 billion) at the end of 1996.
ABN AMRO said total revenue rose 18 percent to 19.0 billion guilders ($9.79 billion) in 1996, with the largest component, net interest revenue, increasing by 12.6 percent.
Interest margins were squeezed by strong competition but this was more than offset by volume growth, particularly in the United States.
"But we also have cream on top of the cake -- commissions and financial transactions," chairman Jan Kalff told reporters.

Financial transactions income soared 57 percent to 1.88 billion guilders ($968 million) and net commissions gained 19 percent to 4.96 billion ($2.5 billion), mainly due to buoyant stock markets and growth in asset management fees.

ABN AMRO set aside provisions of 340 million guilders ($175 million) to adapt computer software for the advent of a single European currency in 1999 and the millennium, projects which it said would cost a total of 500 million guilders ($258 million) over time.
The bank said it was optimistic about its outlook but it was too early to make a forecast of current year results.
"That doesn't mean we would expect a decrease in profits. It's simply not possible to give any statement about the future," Kalff said.
But, echoing the views of U.S. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan, Kalff said uncertainty about future trading had increased in the last six months due to the high level of stock markets.
He said a fall in equity markets would affect the bank's provisions and could have an indirect effect on the general direction of financial markets. "That's a bit worrying," Kalff said.
Peter Thorne of Paribas Capital Markets said Kalff was right to be suspicious of whether the strong increases in commission and trading income which buoyed 1996 results could be repeated in 1997.
"It's a fabulous set of numbers. They have clearly done well from the securities markets...but it's not clear they can do better next year," he said.
